The description 'Twelfth-century Byzantine manuscript the oath was written out in the form of a cross, relating it visually to Christian ideas' and the source 'page 27 of Surgery: An Illustrated History by Ira M. Rutkow, M.D. published in 1993' ('Foto de la Biblioteca Vaticana') support the caption word for word.

Independent: Wikipedia's Hippocratic Oath article captions the same image 'A 12th-century Greek manuscript of the oath in the shape of a cross' and cites DigiVatLib Urb.gr.64, folio 116. The Vatican Library record for Urb.gr.64 (digi.vatlib.it/mss/detail/Urb.gr.64) lists M. Ceresa, 'Il giuramento di Ippocrate nell'Urbinate greco 64' (Studi e testi 477, 2013), which confirms the shelfmark and the Vatican location. That record gives no date, and its bibliography (Canart on Calabrian scriptoria and the 'style de Reggio'; Irigoin on southern Italy) points to a Greek manuscript made in southern Italy, so 'Byzantine' should be read in the broad sense. The twelfth-century date could not be checked against the Vatican catalogue. It rests on Commons/Rutkow, and Wikipedia agrees with it. No change is needed.

The page gives: Date between 1400 and 1404; ink and pigments on parchment; Accession number W.171.114V; Place of creation Utrecht, Netherlands; object history 'Albert, Duke of Bavaria and Count of Holland (1389-1404), Utrecht, ca. 1404-1405, by commission'.

Independent: The Digital Walters description of W.171 (thedigitalwalters.org/Data/WaltersManuscripts/html/W171/description.html) gives the title 'Duke Albrecht's Table of Christian faith (winter part)' and dates it '1400-1404 CE', Utrecht. It calls the book 'the actual copy prepared for the dedicatee of the text, Albrecht of Bavaria, Count of Holland ... dated to 1404 at the latest, when Albrecht died' and lists 'fol. 114v: Title: Episcopal confession before a bishop / Form: Historiated initial "D," 14 lines / Text: Chapter 29'. Every caption claim holds. The rubric legible in the image reads 'Vanden zonden daer alleen die bisscop of aflooest ende absolueert of sijn ghewaerde penitencier', which fits the subject: sins reserved to the bishop.

The caption gives a single auction-catalogue interpretation as plain fact ('because Rashi's concise commentary stops at folio 29a ...'). The only source is the Sotheby's text reproduced in the Commons description ('Bava Batra's length is attributable to the fact that ...'). The tractate's Gemara is long in itself, and no independent source was found that makes Rashbam's commentary the cause of the page count. The explanation is now attributed to that description instead of stated flatly.

It is independently consistent with Wikipedia (Bava Batra: '176 folios ... making it the longest tractate of the Talmud'; 'The commentary of Rashi ... ends at the beginning of chapter 3; its place is taken by that of his grandson, Rashbam'). fieldFixes.caption: An opening of Tractate Bava Batra of the Babylonian Talmud, printed in Venice by Daniel Bomberg in 1522. By number of printed pages Bava Batra is the longest tractate in the Bomberg Talmud. The Sotheby's description reproduced on Wikimedia Commons attributes this to its commentary: Rashi's concise commentary is printed only through folio 29a, after which the less succinct commentary of his grandson Rashbam takes over.

The caption says the twelve articles were proposed 'of which articles three to twelve became part of the Constitution'. That leaves out that Article the second (congressional pay) was ratified on 7 May 1992 as the Twenty-seventh Amendment, so a reader would think only ten of the twelve are in the Constitution. The Commons description the record cites says so itself ('"Article the second" is now the 27th Amendment.' FOUND), and so does the NARA catalogue record (general note: 'Article 2 was finally ratified on May 7, 1992, as the twenty-seventh Amendment to the Constitution. Article 1 was never ratified.').

fieldFixes.caption: The Bill of Rights dated 25 September 1789: the enrolled original of the joint resolution in which the Congress 'begun and held at the City of New-York' proposed twelve articles of amendment to the United States Constitution. Articles three to twelve, ratified in 1791, became the first ten amendments; article two became the Twenty-seventh Amendment in 1992, and article one was never ratified. On this document the First Amendment is 'Article the third', so today's Fourth Amendment appears as 'Article the sixth'.
fieldFixes.rightsEvidence: Commons file page Permission/Licensing: "This work is in the public domain in the United States because it is a work prepared by an officer or employee of the United States Federal Government as part of that person's official duties under the terms of Title 17, Chapter 1, Section 105 of the US Code." Source: "This media is available in the holdings of the National Archives and Records Administration, cataloged under the National Archives Identifier (NAID) 1408042." NARA catalog record NAID 1408042 (catalog.archives.gov, JSON via /proxy/records/search?naId=1408042): coverage date 1789-09-25; scope note "This item is the enrolled original joint resolution of Congress, engrossed on parchment, proposing 12 amendments to the United States Constitution."; general note "Articles 3 to 12, ratified December 15, 1791, by three-fourths of the State Legislatures, constitute the first ten amendments of the United States Constitution. Article 2 was finally ratified on May 7, 1992, as the twenty-seventh Amendment to the Constitution. Article 1 was never ratified." The Commons description says the ten articles became part of the Constitution "in 1794"; NARA gives 15 December 1791, which the caption follows.
